results.content:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in the Democrats’ U.S. Senate primary in Michigan last Tuesday was the latest sign of an emerging kingmaker in U.S. politics – a little-known super PAC that has tapped the wealth of a new cadre of Muslim-American mega-donors to support far-left candidates.
Since it was launched just six months ago, American Priorities has channeled millions of dollars, primarily from donors with Arab, Muslim, and/or Middle Eastern backgrounds, to a string of winning candidates in high-profile races.
Most of the entity-supported candidates are running on various democratic-socialist policies, such as single-payer health care, abolishing ICE, and slashing the military. But one area in which all candidates are aligned, consistent with the PAC’s mission, is in their antagonism towards Israel.
With several such candidates considered locks for the U.S. House in deep blue districts and potentially Michigan’s Senate seat in November, the independent expenditure vehicle is at the forefront of an increasingly politically influential and growing Muslim-American community – one that has ascended as the Israeli-Palestinian Arab conflict has become a central U.S. political issue following Hamas’ massacre of 1,200 Israelis on October 7, 2023.
In some ways, this is a very American story: As new groups of immigrants establish themselves in America, they eventually seek room for their voice in politics and culture. The key issues that have mobilized Muslim-Americans and the positions held by associated organizations, however, are seen by some as radical. Polls show such voters are significantly more hostile towards Israel and Jews, and tolerant toward groups and ideas the U.S. government has linked to terrorism than the general public – views reflected by the insurgent crop of leftist candidates they are increasingly backing.
Sen. Ted Cruz alleges that an effort is underway to, as Muslim Brotherhood leaders pledged in a 1991 memo, “destroy … Western civilization from within.”
A recent Senate Judiciary Committee hearing convened by Sen. Ted Cruz raised a more chilling issue. The Texas Republican alleged, and witnesses concurred that – in a parallel to what has transpired in countries like France, Germany, and the United Kingdom – the Muslim Brotherhood, a subversive transnational Islamist organization, has cultivated an “entrenched institutional network” in America of NGOs, advocacy groups, and political organizations to advance its leaders’ recorded mission to “destroy … Western civilization from within.” That network, terrorism expert Kyle Shideler found, has actively partnered with the Democratic Socialists of America, as part of what Cruz called a “Red-Green Alliance,” that Shideler said is “united around a revolutionary objective advocating for the overthrow of the U.S. Constitution.” Democrats on the panel boycotted the hearing in protest, claiming in a statement the Texas senator was “[s]capegoating Muslims.”
While such partisan conflicts simmer, Muslim-Americans, who represent meaningful percentages of the population in dark blue New York and purple Michigan alike, are buoying the leftists increasingly dominating the Democrat Party. All indications are that this bloc is positioning itself not only to play an outsize role in shaping the next Congress but also in defining the 2028 presidential contest and America’s future.
Pro-Palestinian Leftists
American Priorities was founded in February as a self-styled “countervailing force” to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). Though the largest such group, it is just one of several relatively new PACs with overlapping donors centered on opposition to Israel (see sidebar). The super PAC is led by Hannah Fertig, a strategist self-identifying as Jewish who figured prominently in the 2020 presidential campaign of Bernie Sanders, who is also Jewish and a backer of staunch anti-Zionist candidates. The group’s treasurer is Mark Hanna, an assembly district leader in New York who began his political career as an organizer focusing on Muslim-related issues, including through forming Yalla Brooklyn, an NGO dedicated to mobilizing Arab and Muslim voters. American Priorities has pledged to put up $10 million this cycle to elect Democratic candidates who believe the party establishment is too pro-Israel. AIPAC and its affiliates have also poured tens of millions of dollars into recent election cycles as support for the Jewish state generally has declined – a long-term trend among Democrats correlating with the rise of the anti-Israel progressive left. To support its political claims, American Priorities cites polls showing a majority of Democratic voters oppose U.S. military aid to Israel, are more sympathetic to Palestinian Arabs than Israelis, and shun candidates who accept AIPAC support.
Many of the super PAC’s top donors are first-generation Muslim immigrants who have made their fortunes in the U.S. They include:
- Hussein “Sam” Mahrouq, who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Jordan, and later grew a single car dealership in Texas into Mahrouq Enterprises International, a conglomerate encompassing 25 companies, spanning 3 continents, and employing more than 650 people across the automotive, technology, and real estate sectors.
- Idris and Haroon Mokhtarzada, brothers who as children fled Afghanistan with their family amid Russia’s invasion before settling in the U.S. They became serial entrepreneurs, most notably founding personal finance app Truebill in 2015 – which six years later was sold to the Rocket Companies for $1.275 billion and became today’s Rocket Money.
- Nazar Khan, born in India and who likewise immigrated to the U.S. as a child, commencing a journey that would take him from the University of Pennsylvania to the perch where he sits today as co-founder and chief technology officer of AI energy infrastructure developer and operator Tera Wulf, valued at around $9 billion.
These are highly successful immigrants who, by all accounts, have lived the American dream. Nevertheless, the super PAC they have written six-figure checks to is partnered with groups advocating far-left social and economic policies aimed at fundamentally transforming America, including Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, Leaders We Deserve, and the IMEU Policy Project.
RealClearInvestigations could not reach or did not receive responses to a series of questions posed to Mahrouq, the Mokhtarzada Brothers, Khan and other top American Priorities donors about their views.
For his part, Mahrouq told CNN in connection with a July 2026 report that he believes in “a U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East that respects the dignity of all people in the region.”
“My focus is not partisan politics, but rather promoting policies that strengthen America, encourage opportunity, and serve the interests of American citizens. I believe decisions affecting our country should be made based on what is best for the United States, independent of pressure from any foreign government, foreign interest group or partisan agenda,” he told Jewish Insider via a spokesperson earlier this year.
Some on the right in the U.S. and Israel alike have advocated for phasing out aid — on good faith grounds that it would redound to both countries’ benefit.
In contrast to those boosters of the U.S.-Israel relationship, nearly every candidate backed by American Priorities has characterized Israel as an “apartheid” state engaged in “genocide” in Gaza, downplayed or rationalized the violence of its jihadist foes, and disparaged their primary opponents by accusing them of being “bought and paid for,” directly or indirectly, by the Jewish state.
Some of the candidates it has supported thus far – many of which its donors have also contributed to individually – include:
- Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat’s candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, boosted by $678,000 of support from American Priorities. An Egyptian-American, during the Arab Spring in 2012 he signed a letter backing Egyptian president and Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi against his opponents. In 2022, he compared a proposed ballot measure in Oklahoma prohibiting judges from considering Islamic law in rulings to “the Trail of Tears,” which followed comments in 2021 in which he drew equivalence between the War on Terror and “the decimation of Native Americans, the Transatlantic Slave Trade, Jim Crow segregation, [and] Japanese interment (sic).” He refused to address the U.S. military’s assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader – who had authorized the killing of perhaps 42,000 Iranian protesters in February – so as not to inflame the many “people in Dearborn [Michigan] who are sad.” This past spring he also suggested that a jihadist attack on random members of a West Bloomfield, Michigan, synagogue in March made sense on one level because several of the attacker’s family members – including a brother who was a commander of the terrorist group – had been killed by Israeli strikes in Lebanon. El-Sayed frequently appears with the antisemitic, terror-sympathizing, and Mao-revering streamer Hasan Piker, dismissing criticism of Piker’s assertion that “America deserved 9/11,” as an example of “cancel culture.” El-Sayed’s father-in-law, Jukaku Tayeb, a contributor of $200,000 to a super PAC backing his son-in-law, has reportedly served on the founding committee of the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA) since at least 2007. ISNA was identified as an unindicted co-conspirator in the then-largest terrorism financing case in U.S. history, concerning the Hamas-funding “charity,” the Holy Land Foundation. The organization emerged from the Muslim Brotherhood, which has also helped birth Hamas and other jihadist groups have emerged. El-Sayed previously served as vice president of the University of Michigan’s chapter of the Muslim Students’ Association (MSA), an organization that also has Brotherhood roots and helped birth ISNA. He made his “Trail of Tears” remarks in front of the Council on American-Islamic Relations’ Oklahoma chapter. The candidate has spoken before the national organization at multiple events. CAIR, another unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation case, has been designated as a terrorist organization in several Arab countries along with the states of Florida and Texas. Fox News reported that some 41 individuals linked to CAIR have contributed over $115k to El-Sayed. Sen. Cruz and the witnesses collectively identified each of these entities – ISNA, Muslim Students Associations, and CAIR – as part of what Cruz called an “entrenched institutional” Muslim Brotherhood that sits “[b]ehind El-Sayed’s political rise.”
- Dr. Adam Hamawy, the Democrat’s nominee for Congress in New Jersey’s 12th District, boosted by $1.5 million of support from the super PAC – slightly more than he raised from all direct contributors as of this writing. An Egyptian-American, as a young man the future plastic surgeon sat in on the lectures of, traveled with, and served as a translator for the “Blind Sheikh,” Omar Abdel-Rahman. In 1995, Dr. Hamawy would testify, potentially untruthfully, on his behalf during the terrorism trial linked to the first World Trade Center bombing that resulted in the cleric’s conviction for, among other things, conspiring to bomb six New York landmarks. A year prior, he volunteered as a doctor in Bosnia during the height of the jihadist insurgency there, under the auspices of an NGO in the Benevolence International Foundation subsequently identified as an Al-Qaeda front group. Most recently, he served for several weeks in 2024 at Gaza’s European Hospital, which he called “a completely benign civilian hospital with no tunnels underneath it” – only to be disproven when Israeli forces identified a military base underneath the facility and eliminated senior Hamas leaders operating there, including commander Mohamed Sinwar, brother of October 7 mastermind Yahya Sinwar. Like El-Sayed, Hamawy has defended Piker’s 9/11 comments, stating, “I think we have to put it all in perspective,” and that “I still love the guy.”
- Daria Avila Chevalier, the Democrat’s nominee for Congress in New York’s 13th District, boosted by $1.3 million of support from the super PAC, including spending in opposition to her primary opponent – matching what she raised from all direct contributors as of this writing. A self-described “working-class Dominican New Yorker who has been organizing in upper Manhattan for a fairer, more equitable, and more affordable New York City since she was a teenager,” Chevalier joined an anti-Israel protest in Times Square on Oct. 8, 2023, where participants openly celebrated Hamas’ atrocities from the day before. While an undergraduate, she co-founded the Columbia University Apartheid Divest group, which has endorsed the “total eradication of Western civilization;” she later led the anti-Israel and antisemitic takeover of the campus after the Hamas attack. Chevalier converted to Islam, she says, as a byproduct of her experience interning in Nablus and being surrounded by Muslim activists. The Democrat nominee, who is said to have “oriented her whole adult life around” Palestinian activism, tweeted that “Israel doesn’t exist” amid a series of since-deleted posts.
Democrat Establishment Fears Antisemitic Takeover
Opponents see such candidates’ anti-Zionism as ultimately indistinguishable from antisemitism, with their rhetoric aimed at demonizing and delegitimizing a free and democratic Jewish state. They hear the AIPAC attacks as dog whistles for age-old tropes about cabals of wealthy Jews controlling policymakers, and as insinuating Jewish dual loyalty – ginning up Jew-hatred and sowing domestic discord.
Pennsylvania Democrat Sen. John Fetterman has been perhaps the seniormost party official to make this case, indicating “I’m deeply alarmed by the way the Democratic Party is going after Israel and allowing just rank anti-Semitism to just flourish, you know, on the left and on the campuses too.”
His lower-chamber colleague, Jewish New Jersey Rep. Josh Gottheimer, one of the few other non-lame ducks in Congress to speak out, recently wrote in the Free Press that “Abdul El-Sayed’s victory…is only the latest evidence that my party is being overrun by antisemitism.”
Joel Rubin, the Jewish outreach leader on Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign, has likewise said that “I think what Sanders and the Sanders operation have done is shove into our system the most categorically anti-Israel, antisemitic candidates that we’ve seen in a generation – if ever, certainly within the Democratic Party” – a reference to the Vermont socialist’s leadership on the left.
Outgoing New York Rep. Dan Goldman expressed similar concerns. A noted progressive who is Jewish, Goldman's primary contest came to be defined in part by his pro-Israel positions and AIPAC ties, which his Jewish opponent, American Priorities-endorsed Brad Lander, seized on critically, en route to a 66-34 trouncing of the former Trump impeachment manager. Lander, like many left-wing Reform Jews, has argued that his progressive principles flow from his faith. In contrast to Goldman, speaking before a Queens mosque in May, Lander told worshippers that Israel is committing “genocide in Gaza” and “potentially” in Lebanon, vowing to cut military assistance and partner with the likes of anti-Israel Muslim Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar in Congress. The former New York City comptroller also disavowed AIPAC and pressed Goldman to sign a pledge to avoid taking such outside political support. An event in the waning days of the campaign illustrated its tenor. Goldman patronized a Brooklyn coffee shop with an activist owner. Upon realizing it had served him, the cafe wrote in a public social media post that it does not serve “genocide enablers,” and it would have turned him away had it known. “[W]e don’t need your money (it’s probably coming from AIPAC anyways),” the since-deleted diatribe read. In Goldman’s concession speech, he lamented that “antisemitic tropes and stereotypes, some of which I heard personally on this campaign, will ultimately be the undoing of our democracy if we all don’t lean in and speak out – even if it’s not politically expedient.”
In advance of a recent failed House vote forced by renegade Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to cut foreign military assistance to Israel, Rep. Adam Smith, the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, decried the “tactics used by those on the far left to advocate for cutting off aid to Israel,” indicating he had had his home “vandalized,” his driveway set on fire, and that a staffer had been “physically assaulted.” Smith revealed this intimidation campaign in a post explaining why the avowed “supporter of Israel” would nevertheless be voting in favor of the amendment. Nearly half of House Democrats – more than 100 in all – joined him, in a marked historical shift. Rep. Massie, the sole Republican to vote in favor of the amendment, is one of the few GOP members to receive direct or indirect contributions from American Priorities supporters, alongside anti-Israel former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene.
Dana Nessel, the Democratic attorney general in Michigan - and first Jewish American to hold that post - has raised similar concerns. She recently indicated at an event organized by the Anti-Defamation League that she will not attend her party’s next convention, after a prior one resulted in its selection of a pro-Hezbollah candidate over a pro-Israel Jewish incumbent for Michigan University regent, and attendees heckled El-Sayed primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens. “I don’t feel safe going,” she said.
“I have profound fears about what is going to happen to this state, and what is going to happen to this country if we don’t have a significant change of course,” she added.
For their part, most of the American Priorities-supported and adjacent candidates have denied that they are antisemites, claiming instead that there is a distinction between Jews, the Jews’ ancestral and biblical homeland where nearly half of the Jewish people live today, and its Jewish leaders. “AIPAC and Israel are not the same as Judaism and the Jewish people,” El-Sayed has said. “I love Judaism and I love the Jewish people…And the single most dangerous thing that they’ve tried to tell us is that somehow they can extend the definition of anti-Semitism to include a foreign government and its leaders.” Virtually every candidate has likewise run on some variation of the argument that, as El-Sayed put it in a recent interview, “we send our money abroad to Israel to drop bombs on other people’s kids. That money should be spent here at home.” The Michigander has also called for cutting aid specifically to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE – all countries that have designated the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization.
The Mamdani Effect
These candidates are following in the footsteps of, and in some cases with the blessing of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – whose rise captured the attention and support of several of American Priorities’ donors prior to its launch, including its two biggest backers, Mohamed Waqas Javed and Omer Hasan. Both have contributed over $1 million to the super PAC to date. While little is publicly known about them, they and a third donor, Tariq Afaq Ahmed, who has contributed $500,000, were pre- and post-IPO employees at AppLovin, today one of the world’s most valuable ad tech companies, from which they likely made a fortune. AppLovin has come under scrutiny for, among other things, its funding from Chinese Communist Party-linked individuals and entities. Javed and Hasan burst onto the scene as power players when they each contributed $250,000, the largest such donations, to New Yorkers for Lower Costs, an independent expenditure vehicle supporting Mamdani’s election. Ahmed would contribute $25,000 to the mayor’s campaign.
In the final hours of the Democrat primary, brothers Haroon and Idris Mokhtarzadeh would donate $189,000 to Mamdani. Haroon has created Islamic-centric businesses and participated in explicitly Muslim business forums, and sits on the board of the likes of Israel-hostile Mehdi Hasan’s Zeteo, and Drop Site News, co-founded by jihad-sympathetic journalist Jeremy Scahill. His brother Idris has taken a lower profile, albeit likewise seeking to promote Muslim businesses, via his involvement in Collective Continuum, a group that seeks to “empower 1,000 Muslim-led ventures by 2030.”
American Priorities’ treasurer, Hanna, previously served alongside Mamdani in the 2017 campaign of Palestinian-American Rev. Khader El-Yateem. Mamdani said that El-Yateem “transformed” his life, in part by connecting him with “a political movement that understood Palestine as being a central part of the struggle, which is something that I had often struggled with…all of these politicians I had admired…found every way to not address Palestinians when it came to their seemingly universal struggles.”
The Mamdani campaign, which emerged from the city’s Muslim Democrat establishment and made Israel and the Palestinian Arabs a major focus, appears to have catalyzed Muslim donors nationally, while demonstrating a proof of concept for how targeted contributions could dramatically increase their political clout going forward.
“After Mamdani’s upset victory over the presumed favorite, [former Gov. Andrew] Cuomo, some of those who supported Mamdani told ABC News they felt their contributions toward his victory could forecast a rise in a larger network of Muslim Americans fundraising in national politics, which they say might influence who will run, and who might win,” the outlet reported at the time.
Ahmed, the former AppLovin employee turned angel investor, called the groundswell of national Muslim support behind Mamdani perhaps “the infancy of something to come.”
Palestinian Cause Binds American Muslims and the Left
The Israel-Palestinian conflict is seen as a unifying issue among a Democrat-aligned but ideologically heterodox Muslim American community estimated at somewhere between 3.5 (by Pew) and 8 million (by CAIR) – 60% of whom are immigrants. Writing in City Journal, Zainab Al-Suwaij, co-founder of the American Muslim League, says that for her co-religionists “the Israel-Palestine conflict has become a defining aspect of their identity, though it directly affects only a tiny portion of the community. No one assumed that all Catholics supported the IRA. By contrast, the Palestinian cause attracts millions of Muslim Americans who have nothing to do with the conflict, but who have been told by clerics, community leaders, and professors to think of it as a religious duty.” The war in Gaza ranked as the second most important issue for American Muslims after the economy, at 35%, according to a 2025 Institute for Social Policy & Understanding poll. Likewise, a survey of Muslim-American voters in the 2024 election produced by CAIR found that of all Muslim-related foreign policy issues during that cycle, the most important one to respondents was “Israeli Genocide.”
Suwaij made her assertion in response to polling of Muslim Americans commissioned by her organization. That survey found that among respondents, some 66% support the Muslim Brotherhood, 35% support Hamas, and 17% harbor unfavorable views towards Jews. The Hamas figures dovetail with a Pew poll indicating 44% support among American Muslims – in line with polling of Palestinian Arabs themselves.
Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib, leader of the Atlantic Council’s Realign for Palestine project, says, “Based on countless interactions, trends, and observations since October 7, this number is almost certainly an undercount.” Like Suwaij, he has written that “Many parents import rigid political narratives from their countries of origin and pass them to their children, leaving first‑ and second‑generation Muslim Americans trapped between inherited dogma and their own attempts to think more broadly. The near-absence of healthy institutional infrastructure then reinforces that foundation. National organizations like CAIR, AMP [American Muslims for Palestine], SJP [Students for Justice in Palestine], and MSA have filled the vacuum with grievance‑based politics, enforced conformity, and a culture where dissent is punished as betrayal.” Sen. Cruz and his witnesses also assessed that, like CAIR and MSA, AMP and SJP are Muslim Brotherhood-linked. Shideler, during the Cruz-led hearing, likewise identified Emgage PAC, the self-described largest Muslim American PAC, as linked to the Brotherhood’s U.S. network, noting it “was created by a former CAIR member who at one time was on a terror watch list, and was also a consultant to convicted terrorist Sami al-Arian.” American Priorities donor Khan, among his other Islamic philanthropic pursuits, sits on the board of Emgage Action, that organization’s lobbying and advocacy arm.
The Pew poll also showed that Muslims have a more favorable view of Palestinian Arabs than any other religious cohort at 78%, and a less favorable view of Israelis than any other religious cohort at 26% support. Following the October 7 attack, nearly 58% of American Muslims surveyed found that Hamas was at least somewhat justified in carrying out the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust “as part of their struggle for a Palestinian state.”
Each year, the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) surveys populations around the world using questions to assess animus towards Jews via acceptance of derogatory stereotypes. Globally, in its 2025 survey, the ADL found that 46% of adults harbored antisemitic attitudes. In the predominantly Muslim Middle East and North Africa – comprised of nations rendered virtually judenrein during the 20th century after hundreds of thousands of Jews were expelled or fled under antisemitic threat – that figure rises to 76%. There is little polling on American Muslim views of Jews, but ADL figures from 2017 show that 34% of Muslim Americans held antisemitic views – more than two times the rate of non-Muslims. More recently, a Heritage Foundation poll from September 2024 found that American Muslims believe Jewish people have “too much power” by a rate of 57% to the general public’s 17%.
Manhattan Institute President Reihan Salam, the son of Muslim immigrants, has identified what he sees as two problematic “ideological tendencies” among American Muslims that are of increasing relevance as Islam is set to surpass Judaism as America’s second largest religion within the next generation, and as Muslims’ political power grows. The first is “Islamism” and its violent manifestation in jihad. The second that he hypothesizes persists among upwardly mobile, educated, and often relatively secular Muslims is their rejection of “the quiet gratitude that one associates with immigrants and their children of earlier eras.” This, he says, is not so much due to the dictates of their faith as they understand it, but due to “‘anti-West westernization’ or ‘adversarial assimilation’: a process by which incorporation into American institutions produces not attachment to patriotic narratives of American freedom, individualism, and benevolence but hostility toward them.” He says that this cohort is in thrall to “Third Worldism,” which Salam defines as “a fusion of anti-Zionism, anti-Westernism, and anti-capitalism that places the sacralized victimhood of Palestinian Arabs at the center of a larger struggle against American imperialism.”
Of the two tendencies, “in important respects,” he argued recently in Sapir Journal, Third Worldism “presents the more consequential long-term ideological challenge.”
“Where jihadism targets American civilians as part of a larger struggle to overthrow ‘apostate’ regimes in the Muslim world, Third Worldism endeavors to transform the nation’s ideological-intellectual milieu, shaping how Americans – well beyond the Muslim minority – understand their country and its place in the world.”
This “Third Worldism,” as I detailed in a 2020 book on the growing nexus between Islamic supremacism and the left in the U.S., titled “American Ingrate,” can be traced in part to the Soviet Union’s championing of the Palestinian Arab cause, and the terror fomented by PLO leader Yasser Arafat, during the Cold War – which became a cause célèbres of the global left.
From the Uncommitted Movement to the 2028 Presidency
The Muslim community’s influence on U.S. politics this electoral cycle comes on the heels of the so-called Uncommitted National Movement during the 2024 presidential election.
Led by Lebanese-American political strategist Abbas Alawieh and Palestinian-American activist Layla Elabed, the protest group organized some 700,000 voters to oppose then-President Biden and Vice President Harris in the primary over policies perceived to be too pro-Israel with respect to the war in Gaza. That movement started with 10,000 mostly Arab and Muslim Michigan voters, a swing state consisting of nearly 250,000 Muslims, and grew across the country. El-Sayed himself was among them, supporting the cause. Alawieh ran for state senate in Michigan as a Democrat this cycle and won the nomination. Harris, who is expected to once again seek the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, just endorsed El-Sayed.
President Trump courted such disaffected voters with his own anti-war platform, cutting into Democrats’ generally dominant margins among Arab and Muslim communities in Michigan and helping him win the state in the 2024 election.
A small but loud cohort on the right has sought to put an America First spin on anti-Israel and what some see as antisemitic activism, in advocating against the U.S.-Israel alliance, railing against the so-called “Israel lobby,” and insinuating that Israel and pro-Israel Jews are manipulating U.S. policy to Israel’s benefit. American Priorities-supported Democratic nominee for the U.S. House from Colorado Melat Kiros, who says “there is no greater concern for me than ending the occupation, apartheid, and genocide in Palestine and guaranteeing Palestinians right to self-determination, statehood, the right to return, and reparations for Israel’s crimes,” has bemoaned that when the Democratic Party “refuses to lead morally on this issue, they are “leav[ing] a vacuum for those on the far right” and “letting antisemites on the right co-opt the movement for Palestinian liberation while giving fodder to AIPAC talking points.” But while prominent on the podcast scene and on social media, there are few successful candidates reflecting such views.
By contrast, as Waleed Shahid, former spokesman for the Justice Democrats and Bernie Sanders, now working for Mayor Mamdani, recently tweeted, “The politicians who were supportive of Uncommitted’s primary campaign (Mamdani, [New York congressional nominee Claire] Valdez, Darializa, Lander, Abdul, [Wisconsin Gubernatorial Candidate Francesca] Hong) are ascendant.” Among those candidates running since American Priorities’ establishment, it has supported all of the names referenced by Shahid save for Hong.
In the run-up to the U.S. Senate primary in Michigan, and specifically touting that race, CAIR launched a “Muslims.Vote” platform as a “one-stop hub for civic engagement.” It noted that “With more than 8 million Muslims in America and over 3 million registered voters, our community already has the power to shape elections, especially in key swing states. But millions more eligible Muslim voters must register, show up, and make their voices count.”
Hamawy and Chevalier are slated to serve as the keynote speakers at its forthcoming annual gala.
Meanwhile, American Priorities has made its ambitions clear. In a press release following El-Sayed’s victory, it wrote: “After a string of eight House victories this cycle, the Michigan primary marks [the] first direct statewide challenge to the Democratic establishment with national implications. El-Sayed’s win tonight will force a reckoning within the party over its backward-looking foreign policy and relationship to Israel – just as the contours of the 2028 presidential cycle come into focus.”

Steve Jobs' son thinks San Francisco's pandemic-era real estate slump helped shift Silicon Valley's center of gravity up north.
Reed Jobs said on the Sabrina Halper Show that Palo Alto and the South Bay were "where all the juice was" during his father's career, when companies including Apple, Google, HP, IBM, and Sun Microsystems clustered there.
"And where is the energy now? I would say it has really migrated north of San Francisco," Jobs said, pointing to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Chai Discovery. "The energy is here, and the companies are here."
Jobs, who grew up in Palo Alto and has lived in San Francisco for nine years, said the pandemic "made a lot of office space really cheap" in the city, so although San Francisco "got very dark" as residents and companies departed, the upheaval made it cheaper to launch businesses.
"It was just a natural turning point for the city," Jobs said. "It's really all happening up here in San Francisco."
Affordable office spaces are highly preferred by tech startups. San Francisco itself is seeing the AI boom shift to smaller neighborhoods instead of the traditionally sought-after Financial District. According to a fourth-quarter 2025 report from Cresa, the Design District, for example, where office space costs around $59.53 per square foot, is seeing a startup cluster. By comparison, office spaces in the Financial District and Mission Bay both cost at least $70 per square foot.
Compared to the sparse Mountain View and the sprawling campuses of Silicon Valley, experts in urban planning and innovation have also previously told Business Insider that startups prefer energetic areas, with mixed-use and easily reconfigurable office spaces that don't come at a premium, due to the need to accommodate long work hours and collaboration.
Jobs, 34, is the son of Apple cofounder Steve Jobs and philanthropist Laurene Powell Jobs. He previously led healthcare investing at his mother's Emerson Collective before spinning out Yosemite as an independent firm in 2023. The San Francisco-based venture firm invests exclusively in oncology, combining investments in cancer-focused companies with philanthropic grants for academic research.
"So for me, I love following where the action is," said Reed. "We're building Yosemite to be right in the thick of things. So, we're building it here in San Francisco."
results.summary:
Reed Jobs suggests that San Francisco’s pandemic-era real estate decline catalyzed a shift in the tech industry's center of gravity from the South Bay toward the city.

### Key Points
- Reed Jobs identified a migration of tech energy from Palo Alto to San Francisco, highlighting companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Chai Discovery.
- Pandemic-driven vacancies lowered commercial real estate costs, allowing startups to establish operations in the city more affordably.
- Data from Cresa shows startups are clustering in neighborhoods like the Design District, where office space costs approximately $59.53 per square foot.
- Tech firms are increasingly favoring smaller, mixed-use urban neighborhoods over the traditional Financial District or sprawling suburban campuses.
- Reed Jobs, founder of the oncology-focused venture firm Yosemite, cited the city's renewed momentum as the primary reason for basing his company there.

### Why it Matters
This shift signals a broader trend of tech innovation moving away from traditional corporate campuses toward dense, urban environments that offer flexibility and lower overhead. By prioritizing affordable, reconfigurable spaces, the next generation of AI startups is fundamentally reshaping San Francisco's commercial real estate market.

results.title: The best smart home upgrade for renters costs nothing and leaves no holes in the wall
results.author: Anurag Singh
results.content:
There’s not much you can do with a smart home while renting. Of course, you can use smart bulbs, plugs, and wireless sensors, since they are easy to carry to your next place, but the more interesting upgrades require changes your landlord will notice.
I wanted something that could make my existing setup smarter without adding more hardware, and the answer was already in my pocket. Using the Home Assistant Companion app, I turned my phone into a presence sensor that tells my smart home whether I am home or away. That info can then be used to control lights, plugs, air conditioning, and several other automations. It costs nothing, requires no installation, and leaves me with nothing to repair when I move out.
Your phone already knows whether you are home
Might as well put it to good use
Your phone is always with you, which means it spends a lot of time tracking your location and connecting to familiar Wi-Fi networks. The Home Assistant Companion app can use that information to create a device tracker that updates its status when you enter or leave the Home zone defined in Home Assistant.
This works better than a motion sensor for automations that affect the entire house. You see, a motion sensor knows when someone walks through a room, although a quiet house does not necessarily mean an empty one. Your phone usually stays with you, giving Home Assistant a much clearer signal to switch off the lights, plugs, fans, or air conditioning after you leave.
While this setup works perfectly fine when you live alone, it doesn't when you have roommates or a partner living with you. In that case, you will have to create a person entity for each resident, and everyone who lives with you has to connect their phone and add their tracker to their profile. I somehow convinced my partner to add her phone to this, which has solved a lot for me, but I am yet to figure out what to do for my dog. As you'd guess, he doesn't have a phone, and I don't want the poor boy to struggle when I'm not at home and the lights and everything go off.
It’s also worth noting that phone tracking only establishes whether someone is home. It cannot reliably tell whether you are sitting in the bedroom or walking into the kitchen, so motion and presence sensors are still useful for individual rooms.
You only need the Home Assistant companion app
Nothing else
As you would guess, setting this up doesn't need a lot of things, just your phone and the Home Assistant Companion app. Install the Companion app, connect it to your server, and allow background location access. The app automatically creates a device tracker for your phone, which you can add to your profile under Settings and People. You can check the Home zone on the map at the same time because a very small radius can allow GPS drift to mark you as away while you are still sitting on the sofa.
Your Home Assistant server must remain accessible after the phone disconnects from your Wi-Fi. The easiest option is Home Assistant Claude, but if you want a fully local setup, you can use an external URL or a VPN like Tailscale. Without remote access, the app cannot immediately send location updates once you leave the local network.
To create a departure routine, open Automations & scenes and add a zone trigger. Select your Person entity, choose Home as the zone, and set the event to Leaves. You can then add actions for switching off lights, plugs, fans, or air conditioning. A second automation that uses Enters as the event can handle your return, with conditions based on time, sunset, or temperature. For example, the entrance lights can turn on when you arrive after dark without running the same routine in the middle of the afternoon.
Phone tracking needs a few safeguards
Give Home Assistant unrestricted access
You need to sort a few things before actually using your phone for tracking. Since GPS updates are not always instant, an inaccurate reading can place you outside the Home zone. Android battery restrictions can also create problems by preventing the Companion app from updating its location in the background. You can fix most of that by giving the app unrestricted battery access and allowing background location.
If you want more accurate tracking, you might want to combine the GPS tracker with Wi-Fi or router-based tracking. Home Assistant can consider you home when your phone is either inside the Home zone or connected to the router, then mark you away after both signals agree. This prevents a single delayed or inaccurate GPS update from triggering the departure routine while your phone is still connected to the home network.
I would also add a short delay before switching everything off. Waiting a few minutes has little effect when you have actually left, and it gives Home Assistant enough time to correct a temporary location error. Also, test the routine with lights or fans before extending it to anything security-related.
Use Home Assistant to the fullest
You might be using Home Assistant to automate . When you connect an AI model to your home server, you can control things that aren't otherwise possible with a traditional setup.
results.summary:
The Home Assistant Companion app allows users to transform their smartphones into presence sensors, enabling automated control of smart home devices without requiring permanent hardware installations or landlord approval.

### Key Points
- The Home Assistant Companion app tracks user location via GPS and Wi-Fi to trigger automations when residents enter or leave a defined home zone.
- This method provides a more reliable signal for whole-home automations than traditional motion sensors, which may fail to detect stationary occupants.
- Users must grant the app unrestricted battery access and background location permissions to ensure consistent tracking and prevent system errors.
- Multi-person households can manage automations by creating individual "person" entities for each resident, though pets require alternative detection methods.
- Integrating router-based tracking or adding a short delay before triggering departure routines helps mitigate issues caused by GPS drift or signal delays.
- Remote access to the Home Assistant server, via services like Tailscale or external URLs, is required for the app to report location updates outside the local network.

### Why it Matters
This approach offers a cost-effective, non-invasive way for renters to implement sophisticated smart home automation without modifying their living space. By leveraging existing mobile hardware, users can improve energy efficiency and convenience while maintaining the flexibility to move their setup to a new location.

results.title: What to know about Elon Musk's massive $16.8 billion chip factory
results.author: Max Zahn
results.content:
What to know about Elon Musk's massive $16.8 billion chip factory
The factory is set to be the largest building in the world, Musk said.
Elon Musk plans to build a $16.8 billion chip factory that he says is set to become the largest building in the world.
Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, announced the project as chip manufacturers worldwide ramp up production in response to a surge of demand triggered by advances in artificial intelligence.
The massive plant, known as Terafab, will be located in southeastern Texas, roughly 70 miles outside Houston, according to its website.
"The facility will be an advanced semiconductor fab that will bridge the divide between current global chip supply and the compute demand of the future," the website says.
Here's what to know about the new chip factory:
Why is Elon Musk building a new chip factory?
Semiconductors are a key ingredient in a vast array of products ranging from washing machines to refrigerators to laptops. The growing adoption of AI, meanwhile, has driven up demand for advanced chips.
SpaceX oversees xAI, a Musk-led AI company that offers a chatbot in competition with the likes of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. Those AI ambitions will require data centers equipped with semiconductors.
Tesla-made electric vehicles and humanoid robots will also need chips, the factory's website says.
The combined demand for chips from SpaceX and Tesla is expected to exceed 1 terawatt of compute, a larger amount than the entire global supply currently available, according to the website.
SpaceX and Tesla both rank among the 11 largest companies in the world, as measured by market capitalization. Taken together, they boast a combined value of more than $3 trillion.
What's different about Elon Musk's new chip factory?
The factory will span 100 million square feet of manufacturing space, making it the largest facility of its type in the world, according to its website.
Beyond its size, the website said, the factory will be vertically integrated, meaning it will put each phase of the production process under one roof, including manufacturing, packaging and testing.
The facility will employ 3,000 people, many of whom will be from the local area surrounding the factory site, the website said.
In an effort to mitigate environmental impact, the factory will depend on water from a nearby reservoir rather than local groundwater, the website said.
The plant makes up a a part of Musk's aspiration to build space-bound data centers and other infrastructure in space.
"By building and operating the largest chip manufacturing facility on the planet, we're continuing down a path where future humans can compete over building the largest facilities in the solar system, and eventually the galaxy," the website said.
What's next for Elon Musk's new chip factory?
The multi-billion dollar investment announced by Musk marks the first phase of construction on the plant. A future potential expansion, the website said, could bring "total investment much higher."
In a statement last week, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott applauded the project and hinted at its ever-growing scale.
"Texas is where big ideas grow even bigger," Abbott said.
results.summary:
Elon Musk has announced plans to construct Terafab, a $16.8 billion semiconductor manufacturing facility in southeastern Texas that is projected to become the world's largest building.

### Key Points
- The 100-million-square-foot facility will be located approximately 70 miles outside of Houston.
- Terafab will utilize a vertically integrated production model, housing manufacturing, packaging, and testing under one roof.
- The plant aims to support the massive compute requirements of Musk’s companies, including Tesla’s electric vehicles and the xAI artificial intelligence division.
- The project is expected to create 3,000 jobs and will source water from a nearby reservoir to minimize local environmental impact.
- Musk anticipates that the combined chip demand from his companies will eventually exceed one terawatt of compute power.

### Why it Matters
This massive investment highlights the intensifying global race to secure semiconductor supply chains as artificial intelligence development drives unprecedented demand for high-performance computing hardware. By vertically integrating production, Musk aims to bypass traditional supply bottlenecks and ensure his companies maintain the necessary infrastructure to lead in the robotics and AI sectors.

Nintendo's Switch 2 has been missing something the original console had in spades: flashy special editions. But that could finally change, as leaked images supposedly show a Zelda-themed Switch 2 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the franchise, complete with matching accessories.

results.author: Caitlin Dewey
results.content:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.
It’s not exactly the stuff of Netflix spy thrillers, but…it’s also not every day that the president makes a covert getaway in a catering truck.
White House officials revealed on Monday that, before a flight from Turkey to the United Kingdom last month, President Donald Trump used the truck to secretly move between planes, then switched aircraft again after landing in Britain.
The ruse deceived both Trump’s press corps and many of his staff, who weren’t warned of the last-minute plan in advance. But the deception was undertaken, officials said, in response to an assassination threat from Iran.
Such plots are one tool weaker powers can wield in asymmetric warfare, or conflict between unevenly matched opponents. Iran can’t strike the US homeland with conventional military force the way the US can strike Iran.
As the catering truck caper attests, however, that doesn’t put Americans entirely beyond Tehran’s grasp. Instead, Iran is finding other, less conventional ways to inflict damage on US turf — from assassination plots to cyberattacks.
We might need a bigger catering truck to escape all of that.
“We have more cybersecurity regulations for your credit card than we have for the nation’s water supply.”
— Joshua Corman, founder of I Am the Cavalry, a digital security nonprofit
Iran doesn’t appear able to launch the kind of major cyberattacks that would seriously disrupt Americans’ daily lives en masse. But over the past five months, attacks linked to Iran and pro-Iranian groups have targeted US medical device makers, social networks, public transit agencies, and — most recently, and perhaps most alarmingly — small-town utilities.
Unknown hackers compromised the water and wastewater systems of municipalities in at least 12 states last month, prompting water shut-offs, flooding and boil-water notices in a handful of locations. Cybersecurity experts think Iran is most likely behind the breaches. And American water systems — which are overwhelmingly run by small, local agencies — are especially vulnerable to this type of attack. They have little in the way of IT support, and relatively few state or federal laws require them to take cybersecurity precautions.
It isn’t just utilities at risk, either. Over the past 10 years, Iranian hackers have also breached US targets ranging from satellite companies to political campaigns. And if the war continues to stretch on, some analysts believe the country’s hacks could grow more aggressive.
The Trump administration hasn’t shown any great desire to address this risk, alas. Just a few months ago, it proposed $707 million in cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency — the people responsible for protecting the nation’s infrastructure from cyber threats.

But that deluge of daily data can overwhelm both your mental bandwidth and your mental health. Try letting go of some of these low-stakes tidbits so you can focus on subjects that most deserve your attention.

results.title: Fans Created A 2D Demake Of Metroid Prime In Celebration of Metroid Turning 40
results.author: Ash Parrish
results.content:
Nintendo may have let Metroid‘s birthday slip by unremarked, but a bunch of fan creators didn’t, commemorating the game’s 40th anniversary by releasing Metroid Prime Origins, a 2D remake of Metroid Prime. Spotted by PC Gamer, the demake pixelates the 2002 GameCube game, rendering it in graphics similar to that of its NES ancestor, Metroid.
Last year, Nintendo finally released Metroid Prime 4: Beyond after the game had spent almost a decade in development hell, a period which included at least one development reboot. However, for as generally well-received as the game was, it felt a bit flat compared to the previous games in the Prime series. While Origins is a fan project, it’s at least something to acknowledge and celebrate Samus’ 40th, as apparently Nintendo forgot. A quick check of Nintendo’s website and X page reveals…nothing. Not an acknowledgement of the anniversary, no birthday wishes for Samus, not even a celebratory sale on Metroid Prime 4 or Metroid Dread to mark the occasion.
In a post on Reddit, Origins‘ creators at Lv. 4 Games, a small indie studio that previously made the Castlevania fangame Castlevania ReVamped, say the game took three years to make. They also assured fans that no generative AI was used in the creation of the game. There apparently was a trailer to go along with Origins, but it was removed from YouTube due to unspecified terms of service violations. While the devs say they hadn’t received any cease-and-desists, they know they’re flying too close to Nintendo’s sun, with one member of the team writing in the Reddit post, “I know I am now a target of the Nintendo ninjas.”

- The project reimagines the 3D Metroid Prime experience using visual aesthetics inspired by the original 1986 NES Metroid title.
- Nintendo has not officially acknowledged the 40th anniversary of the franchise or offered promotional sales for recent titles like Metroid Prime 4: Beyond.
- The developers removed their project trailer from YouTube following unspecified terms of service violations.
- The team behind the project expressed awareness of potential legal risks regarding Nintendo’s strict intellectual property enforcement policies.

### Why it Matters
This fan-made project highlights a disconnect between Nintendo’s official marketing strategy and the high level of engagement from the franchise's dedicated community. It also underscores the ongoing tension between independent developers creating tribute content and the company's aggressive protection of its intellectual property rights.

Michael #1: Claude Code /insights
- Michael’s Insights: michael-kennedy-claude-code-insights-2026-08-09.html
- Be careful sharing these outputs, they include details references to your projects, errors, security findings, etc. ;)
- /insights reads your last 30 days of local session transcripts and hands back an interactive HTML report on how you actually work.
  - One command, zero setup: type /insights in a session, or runclaude -p "/insights" from the shell for a non-interactive version that just prints the path
  - Reads what's already on disk: pulls session logs from ~/.claude/projects/ , skipping agent sub-sessions and anything under 2 messages or 1 minute
  - Project areas: clusters your sessions into themes like "CLI Tooling" or "Documentation" with session counts
  - Friction analysis: categorizes where things went wrong by root cause - and quotes your own prompts back at you
  - Interaction style: tells you whether you're a delegator or a micromanager, plus which workflows are worth doubling down on
  - Actually actionable: suggests concrete CLAUDE.md additions and Claude Code features you're not using
  - The catch: Haiku does the per-session classification, so the first run takes several minutes; results cache to ~/.claude/usage-data/facets/ and the report lands at~/.claude/usage-data/report.html
- One command, zero setup: type 
Calvin #2: Post-quantum crypto lands in Python
- pyca/cryptography 48 ships ML-KEM (key establishment) and ML-DSA (signatures) — NIST's post-quantum standards, now onepip install away.
- Big deal because it's the 11th most-downloaded package on PyPI (~1.2B downloads/month) and sits under Ansible, Certbot, Airflow, and paramiko. No PQ there, no PQ anywhere in Python.
- Trail of Bits did the work (Rust bindings, cross-backend API, tests, AWS-LC backend support), funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency.
- Timing tracks a June 22 White House order setting federal deadlines: PQ key establishment by end of 2030, PQ signatures by end of 2031.
- Not a drop-in swap — the wire sizes explode. ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes vs Ed25519's 64; ML-KEM-768 public keys are 1,184 bytes vs X25519's 32. Hardcoded field sizes and length prefixes will bite.
- API looks like the existing asymmetric primitives, except ML-KEM is encapsulate/decapsulate rather than a Diffie-Hellman exchange. SLH-DSA (the hash-based conservative backstop) is still in progress. The primitives are here, but protocols haven't caught up — so you won't be running post-quantum Certbot this week.
Sponsor: Xweather
You're using agents that can write code, summarize documents, and automate workflows. But they're missing one thing: awareness of the world around them. This is where today's sponsor, Xweather comes in. Xweather combines enterprise-grade weather intelligence with agent-ready APIs, natural language capabilities, and an MCP server built for tools like Claude, Codex, Copilot, and modern IDEs – so your agents can adapt workflows, automate responses, and make better decisions based on real-world conditions. Backed by Vaisala, whose instruments fly on NASA missions to Mars, Xweather delivers trusted data and unique insights that go beyond conditions to actual impact – from real-time lightning strikes to road surface forecasts. Start with 15,000 free API calls each month and pay only for what you use as you grow. Xweather is your full weather stack, for developers by developers. Start building for free today at pythonbytes.fm/xweather. The link is in your podcast player's show notes and on the episode page. Thanks so much to Xweather for supporting Python Bytes.
Calvin #3: MCP goes stateless — and FastMCP gets renamed
- From Philipp Acsany over at Real Python
- The 2026-07-28 spec landed July 28 and the Python SDK shipped 2.0.0 the same day. Biggest rewrite since MCP launched, and it's breaking on purpose. Context for scale: the Tier 1 SDKs are pulling close to half a billion downloads a month, with TypeScript and Python each past a billion total.
- The headline is the stateless core. The initialize /initialized handshake and theMcp-Session-Id header are both retired — protocol version, client identity, and capabilities now ride in_meta on every request, with an optionalserver/discover RPC if a client wants capabilities up front. Any request can land on any instance behind plain round-robin, no shared storage.
- Server-initiated calls are the hard part of the migration. Sampling, elicitation, and roots/list no longer call back to the client; instead the server returnsresultType: "input_required" and the client retries withinputResponses attached. Multi Round-Trip Requests, MRTR. Also:Mcp-Method andMcp-Name are now required headers so gateways route on headers instead of cracking JSON bodies, and missing-resource errors move to standard32602 .
- Deprecation sweep with an actual policy behind it — Roots, Sampling, Logging, and the legacy HTTP+SSE transport all deprecated with a twelve-month minimum offramp. Tasks graduated out of the experimental core into a real extension, which is what the formalized extensions framework was for. MCP Apps is now an official extension too, so a tool call can return sandboxed interactive HTML. Auth picked up RFC 9207 issuer validation, issuer-bound credentials, and a shift from DCR toward CIMD.
- Python SDK 2.0 is where it gets personal: FastMCP is nowMCPServer , no alias, no shim.McpError →MCPError . Wire types went snake_case (is_error ,input_schema ) and moved to a standalonemcp_types package, withmcp.types kept as a permanent alias. OneClient object replaces the old transport +ClientSession +initialize() stack.httpx becamehttpx2 . Sync handlers run on worker threads now, soasyncio.get_running_loop() raises inside them.
- The good news: one MCPServer serves both protocol eras, so 2025-era clients keep working with nothing to configure, and aResolve(fn) parameter lets one tool body cover MRTR and the old path. 1.x is maintenance-and-security-fixes only — pinmcp>=1.28,<2 if this week is already full. The Tasks extension isn't in 2.0.0 yet, so Tasks has left the core spec but hasn't landed in the SDK.
If you only call MCP servers, you mostly just get the benefits for free. If you ship one, you already know what your week looks like. And if you use the standalonefastmcp package instead of the official SDK — different project, 3.x line, none of this touches you. The rename is partly to stop the two from being confused.

Scott Bessent endorses Meta’s Muse Glimmer as win for innovation
The US Treasury Secretary backs open-source AI as a strategic priority, praising Meta's latest model release as proof American firms can lead while sharing their work.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thrown his weight behind Meta’s release of Muse Glimmer, a new open-source AI model, calling it a win for American innovation and a bulwark against foreign intellectual property theft. The endorsement ties together two threads that rarely share the same sentence: open-source software philosophy and national security strategy.
Meta launched Muse Glimmer on August 10, 2026, a 30-billion-parameter dense multimodal model built to run locally on consumer-grade GPUs. It ships under the Apache 2.0 license, meaning anyone can use, modify, and distribute it without paying Meta a dime.
What Muse Glimmer actually does
The model is designed for what the AI community calls “agentic workloads,” tasks that run for extended periods, make decisions, and recover from failures without constant human babysitting.
Muse Glimmer supports a context window of more than 120,000 tokens, giving it the ability to hold large amounts of information in working memory during a single session. That context length puts it in competitive territory with several leading commercial models, but with a critical distinction: it runs on hardware people already own.
Meta engineered the model to be compatible with consumer NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple GPUs. Most frontier AI models require data center infrastructure that costs thousands of dollars per hour to rent. Muse Glimmer is positioned as a distilled version of Meta’s larger, closed Muse Spark 1.2 model, trading some raw capability for the ability to run on a desktop machine.
Bessent’s open-source pitch
Bessent’s endorsement went beyond a polite nod. The Treasury Secretary explicitly connected open-source AI development by American companies to the broader goal of protecting US intellectual property from foreign theft.
The geopolitical backdrop matters here. US-China tensions over AI development and intellectual property have intensified steadily, with export controls on advanced chips and growing scrutiny of Chinese AI labs that have been accused of training on proprietary Western datasets. Bessent’s endorsement positions open-source releases not as charity but as competitive strategy.
Meta has been building this playbook for years through its Llama family of large language models, which established the company as the most prominent corporate backer of open-weight AI. Muse Glimmer extends that commitment into multimodal territory, where models process not just text but images, audio, and potentially other data types.
Why the local-first approach matters
Running AI locally instead of through cloud APIs changes the economics and the power dynamics of the technology. When a model lives on your own hardware, your data never leaves your machine. There is no API bill that scales with usage. There is no vendor who can change terms of service or shut off access.
The hardware requirements are still meaningful. A 30-billion-parameter model needs a GPU with substantial memory, likely 24GB or more of VRAM for comfortable inference. That rules out the cheapest consumer cards but sits well within the range of enthusiast-grade hardware from NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple’s M-series chips.
The Apache 2.0 license is also a strategic choice worth noting. Unlike some of Meta’s previous Llama releases, which carried custom licenses with usage restrictions for companies above certain revenue thresholds, Apache 2.0 is one of the most permissive open-source licenses available. There are essentially no restrictions on commercial use.
Meta’s decision to release a distilled version of its larger proprietary model rather than open-sourcing the full Muse Spark 1.2 follows a pattern familiar in the industry. Companies keep their most capable systems behind closed doors while releasing smaller, more efficient variants that demonstrate their technical leadership and build developer loyalty.
The competitive implications extend beyond Meta. OpenAI has moved toward more closed development. Google has released some open models through its Gemma family but keeps its flagship systems proprietary. Anthropic remains entirely closed-source. Bessent’s public endorsement of the open approach adds a layer of political incentive to what was previously a purely business calculation.
